history.heading: Illyrians, Romans and Byzantines
paragraphs: In ancient times the western Balkans were home to the Illyrians, whom many Albanians regard as their ancestors. Greek colonies such as Epidamnos (modern Durrës) and Apollonia were founded on the coast, and the region became part of the Roman Empire in the 2nd century BCE. The Via Egnatia, a major Roman road, began at Durrës.

After the division of the Roman Empire, the area fell under the Byzantine Empire. The name Albanians (Arbanon) appears in Byzantine sources in the 11th century. In the Middle Ages the region was contested by Byzantines, Bulgarians, Serbs, Normans and Venetians, and local Albanian principalities emerged.

history.heading: Skanderbeg and Ottoman rule
paragraphs: In the 15th century the Ottoman Empire expanded into the Balkans. Gjergj Kastrioti, known as Skanderbeg, led a 25-year resistance from 1443 until his death in 1468 and became Albania's national hero. After his death, the Ottomans gained control of the region, which remained part of their empire for over four centuries.

During Ottoman rule, most Albanians converted to Islam, while Orthodox and Catholic communities remained. Many Albanians rose to high positions in the Ottoman state. In the 19th century, the Albanian National Awakening (Rilindja) promoted a common language, schools and national identity.

history.heading: Independence and communism
paragraphs: Albania declared independence in Vlorë on 28 November 1912. The new state faced foreign occupations during the First World War, and was ruled in the interwar period by Ahmet Zogu, who proclaimed himself King Zog in 1928. Italy invaded in 1939, and Germany occupied the country in 1943–44.

Communist partisans led by Enver Hoxha took power in 1944. Hoxha's regime became one of the most isolated and repressive in the world, breaking successively with Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union and China, banning religion in 1967 and building hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers.

history.heading: Democracy and Euro-Atlantic integration
paragraphs: Communism collapsed in 1990–91, and Albania held multiparty elections. The transition was difficult: in 1997 the collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes caused widespread unrest. Large-scale emigration, especially to Italy and Greece, shaped the following decades.
Albania joined NATO in 2009, became an official EU candidate in 2014 and opened accession negotiations in 2022.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Albanian is an Indo-European language that forms its own branch, with two main dialects, Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south; standard Albanian is based mainly on Tosk.

Albania is known for religious coexistence. Muslims, including Sunni and Bektashi communities, form the largest group, alongside Orthodox and Catholic Christians, and many people are not religiously observant. Interfaith marriages and shared celebrations are common.

culture.heading: Traditions and customs
paragraphs: Besa, a code of honour meaning keeping one's word, is a core value; during the Second World War many Albanians sheltered Jews, citing besa. Hospitality is highly valued, and the traditional Kanun, a customary law code, once governed life in the northern highlands.
Iso-polyphony, a form of traditional multi-voice folk singing from the south, is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

culture.heading: Food and heritage
paragraphs: Albanian cuisine is Mediterranean and Balkan, with dishes such as byrek (savoury pastry), tavë kosi (baked lamb with yogurt), fërgesë and fresh seafood on the coast, accompanied by raki.
UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the ancient city of Butrint and the Ottoman-era towns of Berat and Gjirokastër. Mother Teresa, of Albanian origin, is a prominent figure in national pride.

politics.heading: Government
paragraphs: Albania is a parliamentary republic. The 140-member Assembly (Kuvendi) is elected by proportional representation and chooses the president, who has a largely ceremonial role. Executive power lies with the prime minister and the cabinet.
Politics has been dominated by two main parties, the centre-left Socialist Party and the centre-right Democratic Party, often with sharp polarisation. The Socialist Party has governed since 2013.

politics.heading: Reforms and foreign policy
paragraphs: Joining the European Union is the central foreign policy goal. Reforms of the justice system, including the vetting of judges and prosecutors since 2016, and the fight against corruption and organised crime are key requirements.
Albania is a NATO member and has close ties with Kosovo, whose population is mostly ethnic Albanian, as well as with Italy, Greece and Türkiye.

economy.heading: Development
paragraphs: Albania moved from one of Europe's most isolated planned economies to a market economy after 1991. It remains among the poorer countries in Europe, but growth has been steady, and remittances from Albanians abroad are an important source of income.
The currency is the lek.

economy.heading: Key sectors
paragraphs: Tourism has grown rapidly, drawing visitors to the Albanian Riviera, the Alps and historic towns. Agriculture still employs a large share of workers. Industry includes clothing and footwear manufacturing, mining of chromium and other minerals, and oil.
Almost all electricity comes from hydropower. Challenges include emigration of young people, the informal economy and corruption.
